fetched_contents.text: Transfusion thresholds for guiding red blood cell transfusion Abstract Background The optimal haemoglobin threshold for use of red blood cell (RBC) transfusions in anaemic patients remains an active field of research. Blood is a scarce resource, and in some countries, transfusions are less safe than in others because of inadequate testing for viral pathogens. If a liberal transfusion policy does not improve clinical outcomes, or if it is equivalent, then adopting a more restrictive approach could be recognised as the standard of care. Objectives The aim of this review update was to compare 30‐day mortality and other clinical outcomes for participants randomised to restrictive versus liberal red blood cell (RBC) transfusion thresholds (triggers) for all clinical conditions. The restrictive transfusion threshold uses a lower haemoglobin concentration as a threshold for transfusion (most commonly, 7.0 g/dL to 8.0 g/dL), and the liberal transfusion threshold uses a higher haemoglobin concentration as a threshold for transfusion (most commonly, 9.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL). Search methods We identified trials through updated searches: CENTRAL (2020, Issue 11), MEDLINE (1946 to November 2020), Embase (1974 to November 2020), Transfusion Evidence Library (1950 to November 2020), Web of Science Conference Proceedings Citation Index (1990 to November 2020), and trial registries (November 2020). We checked the reference lists of other published reviews and relevant papers to identify additional trials. We were aware of one trial identified in earlier searching that was in the process of being published (in February 2021), and we were able to include it before this review was finalised. Selection criteria We included randomised trials of surgical or medical participants that recruited adults or children, or both. We excluded studies that focused on neonates. Eligible trials assigned intervention groups on the basis of different transfusion schedules or thresholds or 'triggers'. These thresholds would be defined by a haemoglobin (Hb) or haematocrit (Hct) concentration below which an RBC transfusion would be administered; the haemoglobin concentration remains the most commonly applied marker of the need for RBC transfusion in clinical practice. We included trials in which investigators had allocated participants to higher thresholds or more liberal transfusion strategies compared to more restrictive ones, which might include no transfusion. As in previous versions of this review, we did not exclude unregistered trials published after 2010 (as per the policy of the Cochrane Injuries Group, 2015), however, we did conduct analyses to consider the differential impact of results of trials for which prospective registration could not be confirmed. Data collection and analysis We identified trials for inclusion and extracted data using Cochrane methods. We pooled risk ratios of clinical outcomes across trials using a random‐effects model. Two review authors independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias. We conducted predefined analyses by clinical subgroups. We defined participants randomly allocated to the lower transfusion threshold as being in the 'restrictive transfusion' group and those randomly allocated to the higher transfusion threshold as being in the 'liberal transfusion' group. Main results A total of 48 trials, involving data from 21,433 participants (at baseline), across a range of clinical contexts (e.g. orthopaedic, cardiac, or vascular surgery; critical care; acute blood loss (including gastrointestinal bleeding); acute coronary syndrome; cancer; leukaemia; haematological malignancies), met the eligibility criteria. The haemoglobin concentration used to define the restrictive transfusion group in most trials (36) was between 7.0 g/dL and 8.0 g/dL. Most trials included only adults; three trials focused on children. The included studies were generally at low risk of bias for key domains including allocation concealment and incomplete outcome data. Restrictive transfusion strategies reduced the risk of receiving at least one RBC transfusion by 41% across a broad range of clinical contexts (risk ratio (RR) 0.59, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.53 to 0.66; 42 studies, 20,057 participants; high‐quality evidence), with a large amount of heterogeneity between trials (I² = 96%). Overall, restrictive transfusion strategies did not increase or decrease the risk of 30‐day mortality compared with liberal transfusion strategies (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.15; 31 studies, 16,729 participants; I² = 30%; moderate‐quality evidence) or any of the other outcomes assessed (i.e. cardiac events (low‐quality evidence), myocardial infarction, stroke, thromboembolism (all high‐quality evidence)). High‐quality evidence shows that the liberal transfusion threshold did not affect the risk of infection (pneumonia, wound infection, or bacteraemia). Transfusion‐specific reactions are uncommon and were inconsistently reported within trials. We noted less certainty in the strength of evidence to support the safety of restrictive transfusion thresholds for the following predefined clinical subgroups: myocardial infarction, vascular surgery, haematological malignancies, and chronic bone‐marrow disorders. Authors' conclusions Transfusion at a restrictive haemoglobin concentration decreased the proportion of people exposed to RBC transfusion by 41% across a broad range of clinical contexts. Across all trials, no evidence suggests that a restrictive transfusion strategy impacted 30‐day mortality, mortality at other time points, or morbidity (i.e. cardiac events, myocardial infarction, stroke, pneumonia, thromboembolism, infection) compared with a liberal transfusion strategy. Clinical context for why transfusion is needed now

The evidence points to several common causes of dangerously low hemoglobin that make transfusion urgent. Iron-deficiency anemia is one of the most direct causes, and the evidence states that blood transfusions may be given to patients with severe iron-deficiency anemia who are actively bleeding or have significant symptoms [N3-R2]. The broader anemia literature also emphasizes that anemia is defined by reduced circulating red blood cells, hemoglobin, or packed red blood cells, and that transfusions are commonly used for patients with relatively low hemoglobin levels in controlled situations [N3-R1]. Another important context is acute blood loss, which is explicitly mentioned in transfusion guidelines and is a major reason for red blood cell transfusion [N1-R2]. The evidence also notes that patients with symptomatic anemia should be transfused if they cannot function without treating the anemia, and that symptoms may include fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, and other signs of hypoxia [N3-R5].

Which conditions make transfusion urgent? The evidence supports urgent transfusion when hemoglobin is critically low and symptoms are present. In the emergency department context, the initial evaluation is to determine whether the problem is acute or chronic, and transfusion may be needed in patients presenting with acute anemia [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that not all cases of anemia require an ER visit, but some symptoms demand immediate attention, and that transfusion is a possible option for patients presenting to emergency rooms in need of evaluation for both acute and chronic anemia [N4-R3]. In addition, the transfusion-threshold evidence indicates that transfusion may be appropriate when hemoglobin is low enough to warrant intervention, with a restrictive threshold commonly used at 7.0 g/dL to 8.0 g/dL [N1-F1]. That threshold is especially relevant for patients who are symptomatic or whose condition could worsen quickly.

Why some patients need transfusion while others need investigation first? The evidence suggests that transfusion is not always the first step. For example, the emergency-anemia guidance emphasizes that the initial focus is on distinguishing acute from chronic anemia [N4-R1]. Similarly, the transfusion-threshold review says that transfusion decisions depend on the clinical context and that restrictive strategies are used to reduce unnecessary transfusions [N1-F1]. The anemia-and-transfusion evidence also states that most RBC transfusions are prescribed for patients with relatively low hemoglobin levels and only in controlled situations, implying that transfusion is often preceded by assessment [N3-R1]. The NYU Langone blood-bank evidence also underscores that transfusion services are available 24/7, but the broader evidence suggests that transfusion should be guided by clinical need rather than immediate availability alone [N2-R1]. In short, transfusion is urgent when hemoglobin is critically low and symptoms are present, but investigation should come first in patients whose low hemoglobin may reflect a chronic condition, acute bleeding, or another reversible cause [N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3][N1-F1].

Urgent transfusion options and where to go

Which settings can provide an urgent blood transfusion? The evidence shows that urgent transfusion can be provided in multiple healthcare settings. The blood-bank-and-transfusion-services evidence states that NYU Langone’s services are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and that the blood bank provides laboratory support for all transfusions within the NYU Langone Health system [N2-R3][N5-R3]. It also notes that blood bank and transfusion services are located in multiple locations, suggesting broader institutional access [N2-R1]. The evidence on emergency prehospital blood transfusion further expands access by extending transfusion capabilities to rural and remote areas with long transport times, and it mentions improved safe storage and transfusion logistics [N2-R3]. In New Jersey, paramedics are now authorized to provide blood transfusions to critically injured patients under state waivers, which is a direct example of urgent transfusion being available outside the usual hospital setting [N2-R4]. The transfusion-guidelines evidence also indicates that transfusion is part of the emergency department workflow for patients with acute anemia and for those needing evaluation for both acute and chronic anemia [N4-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports that urgent transfusion can be delivered in emergency departments, hospital transfusion services, and, in some cases, prehospital settings such as ambulances or paramedic teams [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N4-R3][N5-R3].

When to prioritize a transfusion versus transfer? The evidence points to two main considerations. First, transfusion is appropriate when hemoglobin is critically low and symptoms are present, especially in acute or severe anemia. The transfusion-threshold review indicates that transfusion decisions depend on clinical context and that restrictive thresholds are used to reduce unnecessary transfusions [N1-F1]. Second, transfer is appropriate when a patient’s hemoglobin is low but the immediate setting lacks capacity, testing, or the right expertise. The physician’s original guidance says that if transfusions are not available nearby, the patient should be transferred to a well-equipped facility [N1]. The emergency-anemia guidance also stresses that the initial evaluation should distinguish acute from chronic anemia, which implies that transfer may be needed if the patient’s low hemoglobin is not immediately treatable in the current setting [N4-R1]. The blood-bank-and-transfusion-services evidence also suggests that transfusion availability is not always universal, and that institutional services can support transfusion 24/7 [N2-R1][N5-R3]. Therefore, the evidence supports prioritizing transfusion when the patient is unstable, symptomatic, or in a setting where transfusion can be provided quickly, while transfer should be considered when the local facility cannot provide safe transfusion or when the patient’s condition requires more specialized care [N1][N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-R1][N5-R3].

First, get the patient to an emergency department or hospital with transfusion capabilities as quickly as possible [N4-R3][N5-R3]. Second, if the patient is outside a hospital, the evidence supports seeking help from prehospital providers, especially in locations where paramedics or ambulance services can provide transfusions [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Third, the evidence from NYU Langone indicates that blood-bank services are available 24/7 and can support transfusions within the institution’s system [N2-R1][N5-R3]. Fourth, the physician’s guidance explicitly recommends checking whether a blood transfusion can be obtained right away and considering transfer if it is not available nearby [N1]. The transfusion-threshold evidence also implies that transfusion should be guided by hemoglobin and symptoms rather than being administered without clinical justification [N1-F1]. The emergency-anemia guidance notes that the initial focus is to determine whether the problem is acute or chronic [N4-R1]. In practice, while waiting for transfusion, the patient should be closely monitored for vital signs, symptoms of worsening anemia, and any signs of acute blood loss [N1][N4-R1]. The evidence also implies that transfusion should not be delayed when the patient is symptomatic and hemoglobin is critically low [N3-R5][N4-R2].

When to call emergency services. The evidence clearly supports calling emergency services when symptoms are severe enough to demand immediate attention. The emergency-anemia source says that not all cases of anemia require an ER visit, but some symptoms do [N4-R2]. The emergency-anemia guidance also states that the initial evaluation should distinguish acute from chronic anemia, and that patients presenting to emergency rooms in need of evaluation for both acute and chronic anemia may benefit from transfusion [N4-R1]. The transfusion-threshold review further indicates that transfusion decisions depend on the clinical context and that transfusion should be guided by hemoglobin and symptoms [N1-F1]. Therefore, the evidence supports calling emergency services if the patient has critical symptoms, acute anemia, or hemoglobin levels that suggest urgent transfusion is needed [N4-R1][N4-R2][N1-F1].

First, transfusion is appropriate when hemoglobin is low enough to cause symptoms and when the patient cannot function without treatment [N3-R5]. Second, transfusion may be appropriate for patients with acute anemia, especially when the problem is acute rather than chronic [N4-R1][N4-R3]. ## Integrated answer to the patient’s question

### What the evidence says
The physician’s original advice was spot on: if a friend has severely low hemoglobin, the first priority is to check whether a blood transfusion can be obtained right away, assess for underlying causes, monitor vital signs closely, and transfer to a well-equipped facility if transfusion is not available nearby [N1]. The search evidence supports that advice in several ways.

## 1) When transfusion is urgent and why
The evidence points to several situations in which transfusion is urgently needed. Iron-deficiency anemia is one of the most direct causes, and the evidence states that blood transfusions may be given to patients with severe iron-deficiency anemia who are actively bleeding or have significant symptoms [N3-R2]. The emergency-anemia guidance notes that the initial focus is to determine whether the problem is acute or chronic [N4-R1]. In other words, some patients may need investigation first, especially if their low hemoglobin may reflect a chronic condition, acute bleeding, or another reversible cause [N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3]. The transfusion-threshold review reinforces that transfusion decisions depend on clinical context and that restrictive thresholds are used to reduce unnecessary transfusions [N1-F1].

So the short answer is: **transfusion is urgent when hemoglobin is critically low and symptoms are present, especially active bleeding or signs of acute anemia** [N3-R2][N3-R5][N4-R1]. But **not all low hemoglobin means transfusion right away**; some cases require first determining the cause [N3-R1][N4-R1].

## 2) Where to go for urgent transfusion
The evidence supports several urgent transfusion settings.

### a) Emergency department / hospital transfusion services
The evidence shows that emergency departments can provide transfusion for patients with acute anemia and for those needing evaluation for both acute and chronic anemia [N4-R3]. NYU Langone’s blood bank and transfusion services are also available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and the blood bank provides laboratory support for all transfusions within the NYU Langone Health system [N2-R1][N5-R3]. That means many hospitals have institutional transfusion services that can act quickly.

### b) Prehospital settings
The evidence also expands access beyond the hospital. Emergency prehospital blood transfusion can extend transfusion capabilities to rural and remote areas with long transport times, and it mentions improved safe storage and transfusion logistics [N2-R3]. In New Jersey, paramedics are now authorized to provide blood transfusions to critically injured patients under state waivers [N2-R4]. That is a concrete example of urgent transfusion being available outside the usual hospital setting.

### c) Transfer if transfusion is not available nearby
The physician’s guidance is reinforced by the evidence: if transfusions are not available nearby, the patient should be transferred to a well-equipped facility [N1]. The evidence also supports that transfusion availability is not always universal, and that institutional services can support transfusion 24/7 [N2-R1][N5-R3]. So when nearby access is limited, transfer becomes the right choice.

## 3) Practical steps to get transfusion help immediately
The evidence suggests a clear practical plan:

### Step 1: Assess urgency and symptoms
Check whether the friend is symptomatic. The evidence indicates that patients with symptomatic anemia should be transfused if they cannot function without treating the anemia, and that symptoms may include fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, and other signs of hypoxia [N3-R5]. If the friend is critically low and symptomatic, urgent action is needed.

### Step 2: Seek the nearest emergency facility or prehospital provider
If the friend is outside a hospital, the evidence supports seeking help from prehospital providers, especially in locations where paramedics or ambulance services can provide transfusions [N2-R3][N2-R4]. If inside a hospital, the emergency department is the usual first destination for transfusion [N4-R3].

### Step 3: Check transfusion availability
The evidence emphasizes that transfusion services are available 24/7 in some systems [N2-R1][N5-R3]. However, availability may vary by region and hospital, so checking local capabilities is important [N2-R1][N5-R3].

### Step 4: Transfer if transfusion is not available nearby
If the local facility cannot provide safe transfusion, the evidence supports transferring to a well-equipped facility [N1]. The evidence also supports distinguishing acute from chronic anemia as part of the initial evaluation, which may guide whether transfer is needed [N4-R1].

## 4) What to do while waiting for transfusion
The evidence supports close clinical monitoring and supportive care while waiting for transfusion. The emergency-anemia guidance notes that the initial focus is to determine whether the problem is acute or chronic [N4-R1]. The transfusion-threshold evidence also emphasizes that transfusion decisions depend on clinical context and that restrictive thresholds are used to reduce unnecessary transfusions [N1-F1]. In practice, while waiting, the friend should be monitored for vital signs and signs of worsening anemia [N1][N4-R1]. If symptoms are severe enough to demand immediate attention, emergency services should be called [N4-R2].

## 5) How to evaluate whether a transfusion is appropriate
The evidence provides several criteria for deciding whether a transfusion is appropriate:

- **Symptoms**: If the patient is symptomatic and cannot function without treatment, transfusion is appropriate [N3-R5].
- **Acute anemia**: Transfusion may be appropriate for patients with acute anemia [N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Hemoglobin level**: The transfusion-threshold evidence supports using a restrictive strategy with hemoglobin thresholds of 7.0 to 8.0 g/dL in many clinical contexts [N1-F1].
- **Underlying cause**: Transfusion should not be given without first investigating acute versus chronic anemia and identifying any underlying causes [N3-R1][N4-R1].

In other words, transfusion is appropriate when hemoglobin is critically low and symptoms are present, but it should be guided by clinical context and not given as a routine response to low hemoglobin alone [N1-F1][N3-R1][N4-R1].

## Final practical answer
Here is a clear, patient-facing summary:

1. **Check for urgent symptoms.** If the friend is critically low and symptomatic, urgent transfusion is likely needed [N3-R5].
2. **Go to the nearest emergency department or call emergency services.** Emergency departments can provide transfusion for acute anemia [N4-R3], and emergency services are appropriate when symptoms demand immediate attention [N4-R2].
3. **Check if transfusion can be done right away.** Some hospitals and blood-bank services are available 24/7 [N2-R1][N5-R3].
4. **Transfer if transfusion is not available nearby.** If transfusions are not available nearby, transfer to a well-equipped facility [N1].
5. **Monitor closely while waiting.** Watch for vital signs and worsening symptoms [N1][N4-R1].
6. **Investigate first if the situation is unclear.** Not all low hemoglobin means transfusion immediately; some cases need first determining whether the problem is acute or chronic [N3-R1][N4-R1].

## Bottom line
The physician’s advice is well supported by the evidence. A friend with dangerously low hemoglobin should be treated urgently if symptoms are present, and the best places for transfusion are emergency departments, hospitals with transfusion services, and, in some cases, prehospital providers [N1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N4-R3]. If transfusion is not available nearby, transfer to a better-equipped facility is the next step [N1]. While waiting, the friend should be closely monitored, and transfusion should be guided by symptoms, hemoglobin level, and clinical context [N1-F1][N3-R5][N4-R1].
